intro:
The article analysis question (AAQ) gives you one study and asks six things about it: the research method, an operational definition, what a statistic shows, an ethical guideline the researchers applied, whether the results generalize, and whether the results support the hypothesis. It is worth 7 points, and each part has its own trap.

Pick a part to see exactly where in the summary its answer is, then what earns the point and what the readers saw students miss. Change the result to see how parts C and F change with it.
howItWorks:
Every study here is invented for practice, written in the layout the exam uses: Introduction, Participants, Method and Results with a graph. The numbers are generated each time you run the study and are computed with the course's statistics code, so the graph, the results text and the answers always agree.

The slips under each part come from the College Board's 2025 Chief Reader Reports and the 2025 and 2026 scoring guidelines, in our own words: the wrong or several methods, a definition of the concept instead of how the study measured it, numbers restated instead of interpreted, an ethical guideline the summary never describes, generalizing from sample size, and a claim that a study proves an idea.

contexts.title: Sleep and memory for word pairs
contexts.methodWhy: The researchers manipulated how much the students slept and randomly assigned them to the two groups.
contexts.ivWhat: whether a student slept a full night or was kept awake until 4 a.m.
contexts.intro: Sleep may help the brain hold on to what was learned during the day.
contexts.hypothesis: students who sleep a full night after learning recall more word pairs the next morning than students kept awake for most of the night
contexts.design: Participants were randomly assigned to a full-sleep group or a short-sleep group.
contexts.procedure: At 9 p.m. every participant studied 40 word pairs (such as ocean / ladder) in a sleep lab. The full-sleep group slept from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m.; the short-sleep group was kept awake with quiet activities until 4 a.m. and then slept until 7 a.m.

participants.html: Sixty university students (ages 18 to 22) at one university in Ohio, recruited through an introductory psychology course; 34 women and 26 men.
table: An introductory psychology course in Ohio

dv.name: recall
dv.what: the number of word pairs (out of 40) a participant completed correctly when shown the first word
dv.howNear: right after studying the list at 9 p.m.
dv.vague: how well the students remembered the words
dv.near: the hours each student slept, from a sleep tracker
dv.sentence: At 9 a.m. the next morning, each participant saw the first word of each pair and wrote the second; recall was the number of pairs completed correctly (0 to 40).
dv.res: {g} recalled a mean of {m} word pairs

ethics.how: Before the study, the students signed a consent form that described the overnight stay and the sleep loss.
Students were told they could leave at any time, even during the night, and still receive their course credit.
The university's institutional review board approved the study before it began.

generalize.because: every participant was a university student aged 18 to 22, and both sleep and memory change with age.

generalize.pop: first-year students at other US universities
generalize.because: the participants were 18- to 22-year-old university students in an introductory course, much like first-year students elsewhere in the US.

contexts.flaw: the students knew which group they were in.

contexts.title: Caffeine and nightly sleep
contexts.methodWhy: The researchers measured caffeine and sleep in each person as they were and related them with r; nothing was manipulated and no one was assigned to a condition.
contexts.ivWhat: the milligrams of caffeine a participant took in per day, from a two-week drink diary
contexts.intro: Caffeine is a stimulant, and many adults have it every day.
contexts.hypothesis: adults who take in more caffeine sleep fewer hours per night
contexts.design: The researchers measured each participant's caffeine intake and sleep without changing either.
contexts.procedure: For two weeks, participants recorded every drink with caffeine in a diary, which the researchers converted to milligrams per day.

participants.html: Forty adults (ages 25 to 50) who worked day shifts at one hospital in Atlanta; 26 women and 14 men.
table: Day shifts at one hospital in Atlanta

dv.name: sleep time
dv.what: the average hours of sleep per night
dv.how: recorded by a wrist sleep tracker over the same two weeks
dv.howNear: reported by each participant in one interview at the end
dv.near: the number of cups of coffee each participant drank
dv.sentence: Each participant wore a wrist sleep tracker for the same two weeks; sleep time was the average hours of sleep per night.

ethics.how: Participants signed a consent form that explained the drink diary and the sleep tracker.
Diaries and tracker data were labeled with code numbers instead of names.

generalize.because: every participant worked day shifts, and night-shift workers sleep on a different schedule.

generalize.pop: adult day-shift hospital workers in other US cities
generalize.because: the participants were 25- to 50-year-old day-shift hospital workers.

contexts.flaw: the diaries depended on participants remembering every drink.

contexts.title: Practice quizzes, rereading and highlighting
contexts.methodWhy: The researchers manipulated the study activity and randomly assigned students to the three conditions.
contexts.ivWhat: which study activity a student was given: practice quizzes, rereading or highlighting
contexts.intro: Students often reread or highlight a text, but answering questions from memory may build stronger memories.
contexts.hypothesis: students who take practice quizzes on a text score higher on a test one week later than students who reread it
contexts.design: Students were randomly assigned to one of three study conditions.
contexts.procedure: Each student read a 900-word passage about volcanoes for 10 minutes. Then, for 20 minutes, the quiz group answered short practice questions about the passage, the reread group read it again, and the highlight group reread it with a highlighter.

participants.html: Ninety high school juniors (ages 16 and 17) from two public schools in Texas; 48 girls and 42 boys.
table: Two public high schools in Texas

dv.name: test score
dv.what: the number of questions (out of 30) a student answered correctly on a short-answer test about the passage
dv.how: one week after the study session
dv.vague: how much the students learned about volcanoes
dv.near: the minutes each student spent studying at home
dv.sentence: One week later, every student took the same 30-question short-answer test on the passage; the score was the number answered correctly (0 to 30).

ethics.how: A parent or guardian of each student signed a permission form before the study.
Each student also agreed in writing after a researcher explained the study in plain words.
Test scores were stored under code numbers, and teachers never saw individual results.

generalize.because: all participants were 16- and 17-year-olds in two Texas public schools, so differences in age and school culture could change how students study.

generalize.pop: high school juniors in other US public schools
generalize.because: the participants were 16- and 17-year-old juniors from two US public schools, the same age and kind of school.

contexts.flaw: the test used only one passage, about volcanoes.

contexts.title: Points for reading at home
contexts.methodWhy: The researchers manipulated whether students earned points and randomly assigned them to the two groups.
contexts.ivWhat: whether a student earned points toward small prizes for reading
contexts.intro: Schools often reward reading. A reward that follows a behavior may make the behavior more frequent.
contexts.hypothesis: fourth graders who earn points toward small prizes for reading at home log more minutes of reading than fourth graders who earn no points
contexts.design: Students were randomly assigned to a points group or a no-points group.
contexts.procedure: For four weeks, students in the points group earned one point for every 15 minutes of reading at home and could trade 10 points for a small prize such as a bookmark. Students in the no-points group kept the same reading log with no points.

participants.html: Sixty-four fourth graders (ages 9 and 10) from three elementary schools in a suburb of Minneapolis; 30 girls and 34 boys.
table: Three suburban elementary schools near Minneapolis

dv.name: reading time
dv.what: the total minutes of reading a student logged, with a parent's signature on each entry
dv.how: added up over the four weeks of the program
dv.howNear: counted only in the week after the program ended
dv.vague: how motivated the students were to read
dv.near: the number of books each student owned at home
dv.sentence: Students recorded each reading session in a log that a parent signed; reading time was the total minutes logged over the four weeks.

ethics.how: Parents received a letter about the program and signed a permission form before their child took part.
Each child agreed to take part after a teacher explained the reading log in plain words.
Families were told that a child could stop at any time with no effect on grades.

generalize.because: every participant was a 9- or 10-year-old fourth grader, and older students may respond differently to small prizes.

generalize.pop: fourth graders in other US suburban schools
generalize.because: the participants were 9- and 10-year-old fourth graders from three suburban US schools.

contexts.flaw: parents might have signed some logs without checking them.

contexts.title: Runners on a park trail
contexts.methodWhy: The researchers watched and timed runners in a public park without stepping in; nothing was manipulated, and runners chose whether to run near others.
contexts.iv: whether another runner was in view
contexts.ivWhat: whether another runner was within about 20 meters of the runner
contexts.intro: People sometimes perform simple, well-practiced tasks faster when others are around.
contexts.hypothesis: runners cover a marked 200-meter stretch faster when another runner is in view than when they are alone
contexts.design: The researchers observed runners in their natural setting and did not interact with them.
contexts.procedure: On weekday mornings, two observers on a bench noted whether another runner was within about 20 meters of each runner who passed.

participants.html: Eighty adult runners (estimated ages 20 to 60) on a public trail in one Denver park, observed on weekday mornings in May. Runners were not approached.
table: One public park trail in Denver

groups.name: runners with another runner in view
groups.label: Runner in view

dv.name: running speed
dv.what: the time in seconds a runner took to cover a marked 200-meter stretch of the trail
dv.how: timed with a stopwatch by an observer who did not speak to the runner
dv.howNear: read from each runner's own fitness watch
dv.vague: how hard the runners were trying
dv.near: how many other people were in the park that morning
dv.sentence: The observers timed each runner over a marked 200-meter stretch with a stopwatch; a shorter time means a faster runner.

ethics.how: A university review board approved observing public behavior before the study began.
The observers recorded no names, photos or descriptions that could identify a runner.

generalize.pop: people who do not run for exercise
generalize.because: everyone observed was an adult who chose to run on a park trail, and regular runners may react to others differently than non-runners do.

generalize.pop: adult runners on other city park trails in the US
generalize.because: the participants were adult runners, about 20 to 60 years old, on a public city trail.

contexts.flaw: the observers estimated the runners' ages by eye.

contexts.title: A walk before a stressful task
contexts.methodWhy: The researchers manipulated whether participants walked or sat and randomly assigned them to the two groups.
contexts.ivWhat: whether a participant walked briskly or sat quietly for 20 minutes
contexts.intro: Physical activity may change how strongly people react to a stressor.
contexts.hypothesis: adults who walk briskly for 20 minutes before a stressful task report less stress during the task than adults who sit quietly
contexts.design: Participants were randomly assigned to walk briskly on a treadmill or to sit quietly, each for 20 minutes.
contexts.procedure: Then every participant did the same five-minute timed mental-math task while a researcher watched.

participants.html: Fifty adults (ages 30 to 55) who worked in offices in Seattle, recruited through a newspaper ad; 28 women and 22 men.

dv.name: stress
dv.what: a rating from 1 (no stress) to 10 (extreme stress) of how stressed the participant felt
dv.how: given right after the five-minute timed math task
dv.howNear: given on the morning before the session
dv.vague: how anxious and tense the participants were
dv.near: each participant's heart rate during the walk
dv.sentence: Right after the math task, each participant rated how stressed they felt from 1 (no stress) to 10 (extreme stress).

ethics.how: Participants were not told at first that the math task was meant to be stressful; afterward, a researcher explained the true purpose and answered questions.
Participants could stop the math task at any moment without losing their payment.
Participants signed a consent form that described a walk or rest, a math task and a questionnaire.

generalize.because: every participant was an office worker aged 30 to 55, and younger people with different routines may respond differently.

generalize.pop: adult office workers in other US cities
generalize.because: the participants were adults aged 30 to 55 who worked in offices in a large US city.

contexts.flaw: the participants knew whether they had walked.
